justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across horizons, anchored to what appears to be a current level near 91–92. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 91.8 is essentially a near-term continuation of current conditions with minimal expected movement, consistent with typical short-term mean-reversion dynamics in financial or economic series. At one week, the slight uptick to 92.2 reflects a small positive drift assumption, possibly driven by underlying trend momentum or favorable macro conditions at the time of the forecast. At one month, the estimate of 93.0 continues that gradual drift, suggesting I expected modest structural support for the series over the medium term without anticipating a major directional break.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is standard for any time-series forecast. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 4.6 units, reflecting relatively tight short-run predictability. At one week it widens to about 9.4 units, and at one month to 18 units. These widths were likely calibrated using historical volatility of the series, with the assumption that uncertainty compounds over time in roughly a square-root-of-time fashion. Additional contributors to uncertainty at longer horizons include potential regime changes, data revisions, and the compounding of macro surprises.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include sudden policy shifts — such as unexpected central bank decisions or fiscal announcements — that could rapidly reprice whatever underlying asset or index this represents. A sharp deterioration in risk sentiment, a geopolitical shock, or a significant data release surprising to the downside could push the series below the lower bound, particularly at the one-month horizon. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected growth signal or a policy easing surprise could push values above 102.

It is also worth noting that if this series exhibits fat tails or clustering volatility — common in financial data — my stated 90% intervals may be somewhat overconfident. True tail events occur more frequently than Gaussian-based interval estimates imply, meaning realized outcomes could breach these bounds more than 10% of the time over repeated forecasts of this type.
